doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Standing of the Ellington band and the Richmond Club engagement
summary: Musicians looked up more to Henderson's band; Carter recalls mostly Ellington's own music at a club on 57th Street.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: When you played with Ellington . . . well, first, before we talk about that, we discussed what it meant to play with Fletcher Henderson in 1926, being a sign that you had arrived as a musician and you were accepted. What sort of aura did the Ellington band have at that time among musicians?

I don’t know. Of course, the Ellington Orchestra was the most original of its time, I think, you know. But I think musicians looked up more to the [Fletcher] Henderson Orchestra and its players. Couldn’t tell you why, but I think that was the feeling.
Do you remember anything about the music that you played with Ellington? Was it his own mostly?
Oh yes, it was his own mostly, but gee, that’s . . . I don’t remember. I don’t remember.
And where, which hall or club was this?
It was called the Harry Richmond [phonetic] Club on 57th Street.

Well, I don’t know. I may be wrong, but I keep thinking it was Harry Richmond’s, but, you know, my memory is faded. [Interviewer laughs.] But I’ve always thought it was Harry Richmond’s. I don’t know.
I don’t know where I got Cyro’s.
It might have been Cyro’s. It doesn’t sound unfamiliar, you know.
